title: The two-sided power of subscription
content:
You can get this blog delivered to you every day, for free. The details are here: [https://seths.blog/subscribe/](https://seths.blog/subscribe/)

You can subscribe to streaming channels like Dropout (a new unscripted game show every time), MHz or RetroCrush (rare anime).

You can subscribe to Apocabox if you’re a prepper in need of more stuff, or History by Mail, which will send you facsimiles of historical documents.

And of course, you can subscribe to [Elle Cordova](https://www.youtube.com/@ElleCordova/shorts) on YouTube.

But why? In an instant-on, find-what-you-want world, why spend the time or the money?

Two things happen.

The immediate one is that subscriptions are an asset and a signal. The creator of the product or service is more likely to do the work you seek if you give them a reliable way to get the work out there. This is why Google and others fight so hard to break the connection–they want to own your attention instead.

The long-term one is that the arrival of your subscription is a prompt. It shows up on its schedule, not yours. It’s not just a reminder, it creates a pattern. Seventy years ago, a stack of _Readers Digest_ or _National Geographic_ magazines was a signal to visitors and to the homeowner as well. The same for the _New Yorker_ twenty years ago. And not just for the cartoons.

If you’re already a subscriber to the blog, thanks. If it hasn’t been getting to you, please check your promo folder or resubscribe. And mostly, please forward this to someone who might want to join in. When your colleagues subscribe too, you have a shared prompt to riff on.

Bonus:

My [RSS](https://seths.blog/2011/01/in-defense-of-rss/) reader is a treasure box of _hundreds_ of subscriptions. The blog posts and the occasional [XKCD](https://xkcd.com/) have enriched my life and knowing that more will come opens up anticipation and creativity on my part.

When in doubt, subscribe.

The only way for something you create to be your best work is for everything else to be “not my best work.”

That’s okay. Half of all blog posts are below average, after all.

We can work to relentlessly raise the average. We can forgive the efforts that aren’t the best. And we can set aside our fear of failure (and success) to find the guts to create the next thing that will become our best work. So far.

title: Meet the Bugs That Live in Your Home
content:
As you prepare to celebrate Thanksgiving, a new paper [published](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecy.70628) in _Ecology_ is revealing the many uninvited guests that may be lurking. It’s the largest study to date of the insects, spiders, and other bugs that populate our homes, offices, and other spaces.

“Our goal with this work was to treat the indoors, at the continental scale, as an ecosystem that we wanted to explore as ecologists,” study author Bradley Allf, now at Colorado State University, explained in a [statement](https://news.ncsu.edu/2026/11/creatures-that-live-in-our-homes/).

**Read more: “[5 Devious Ways People Made Bugs Into Bombs](https://nautil.us/5-devious-ways-people-made-bugs-into-bombs-1211227)”**

To catalog the various microfauna of the household biome, an international team of biologists relied on its megafauna—us. They created a citizen science project called [Never Home Alone](https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/never-home-alone-the-wild-life-of-homes) through the iNaturalist app, and asked users to submit photos and videos of the critters they found scurrying around their houses. Altogether, they received nearly 24,000 reports from the United States and Canada, which they then had to comb through to properly identify the species

So what did they find?

The most common household bug was also the charismatic mascot of friendly insects: the ladybug (_Harmonia axyridis_). One notch down the ladder was the slightly less friendly brown marmorated stink bug (_Halyomorpha halys_). Originally native to Asia, this invasive species first popped up in Pennsylvania in 1998 and has spread throughout North America since, plaguing crops as it went. The odor it emits when threatened is reminiscent of cilantro and is especially noisome to people with the [gene variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OR6A2) that makes the herb taste like soap.

Next on the list was the house centipede (_Scutigera coleoptrata_). This many-legged nightmare may look heinous, but it actually hunts and kills other household pests like cockroaches, bed bugs, and termites. You can also tell how old they are by the number of legs. The nymphs are born with just eight, but gain two more each time they molt, maxing out at 30 (though it may seem like more when you spot one climbing up a wall).

From there, the carpet beetle, a mostly benign household critter, was followed by several spiders, all of which help keep other arthropod populations in check (including by eating each other). The long-bodied cellar spider (_Pholcus phalangioides_) and combfoot spider (_Steatoda triangulosa_) are responsible for pesky cobwebs in the corners, while the Eastern parson spider (_Herpyllus ecclesiasticus_) and bold jumping spider (_Phidippus audax_) are more free-ranging predators.

The most common invertebrates in U.S. and Canadian indoor areas. _Credit: Alif et al. Ecology, 2026_

Rounding out the top ten was another semi-invasive species, the Western conifer seed bug (also known as the pine beetle). Originally native to the Western United States, these true bugs are now all over the East Coast. While they’re also harmless, their mouthparts are sharp enough to pierce trees, and they’ve been known to cause leaks with errant jabs into flexible plumbing tubing.

But why catalog the creatures living in our homes anyway?

Well, now that they’ve assembled this vast dataset, other researchers can utilize it to answer a variety of questions. “It could inform future research in many ways,” study author Rob Dunn explained. “For example, we now know that camel crickets carry a microbe that can break down paper products. That could be useful. What else might be out there, in our own homes?”

And if you’d like to help, you still can. “People can still submit observations to [Never Home Alone](https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/never-home-alone-the-wild-life-of-homes),” Allf says. “The more data the project collects, the more insight we’ll have on the unique and growing ecosystem of the great indoors.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Siberian Cranes Made a Massive Comeback—Only to Face a Set of New Threats
content:
Siberian cranes have been lauded as a recovery success story. In 1981, their populations had crashed to just 140 birds after major losses of their wetlands and hunting along their migration routes. But by 2026, they’d recovered forty-fold—with their numbers now totaling more than 5,600. The remarkable comeback was attributed to the protections gained by the [IUCN listing](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22692053/134180990) Siberian cranes (_Leucogeranus leucogeranus_) as Critically Endangered.

The story, however, isn’t so simple.

A [recent perspective](https://www.cell.com/the-innovation/fulltext/S2666-6758(25)00371-6) published in the journal _The Innovation_ looked deeper than the numbers to assess how Siberian cranes were faring. Cranes breed in Russia’s Arctic tundra, then migrate several thousand miles to winter in China. With the degradation of natural wetlands, most congregate at two farmland sites around Poyang Lake in southeastern China. There, in the rice paddies and lotus ponds, they find plenty of food, including water chestnut roots, water hyacinth, and lotus roots.

**Read more: “**[**The Crowd-Sourced Science to Save Endangered Succulents**](https://nautil.us/the-crowd-sourced-science-to-save-endangered-succulents-1279463)**”**

But, according to the study authors from Jiangxi Agricultural University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, cranes’ human-made habitats are rife with antibiotic residues and microplastics as well. The study authors detected water concentrations of the antibiotics azithromycin at 882.6 ng/g and erythromycin at 1,182.5 ng/g, both “far exceeding the commonly recognized safety threshold of 100 ng/g.”

Moreover, in analyzing crane feces under a microscope, the researchers found an average of 62 microplastic pieces per gram of poop, which can disrupt their gut microbiota. The study authors also expressed concern about increased exposure to viruses from other birds that use rice paddies, such as the greater white-fronted geese (_Anser albifrons_), which had the virus causing Newcastle disease (_Orthoavulavirus javaense_) that spreads from poultry into the wild, in their fecal samples.

As such, the researchers argue that “protecting endangered species requires a paradigm shift from counting individuals to understanding population health.” In the paper, they propose a six-dimensional framework for assessing the conservation status of animals that accounts for demography, environment, disease, genetics, physiology, and behavior.

It’s yet another case of numbers not telling the whole story. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Quest to Understand a Tick-Borne Allergy to Red Meat
content:
_[This story](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/health-disease/2026/red-meat-allergy-how-ticks-spread-alpha-gal-syndrome) was originally published by_[Knowable Magazine](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/society/2026/prehistory-lost-threads)_._

Sandra Tiguila, an adventurous eater, enjoyed a bison sausage breakfast sandwich while dining out in August of 2025. On the drive home, she noticed a rash appearing on her wrist. The burning sensation spread to her arms and legs, making it nearly impossible to sleep. In the days to come, she tried creams, pills, injections; nothing helped.

Ten days later, Tiguila ate out again, ordering a steak. When her face swelled up, her boyfriend drove her to the emergency room. A doctor tested her for diseases carried by ticks. Tiguila, who lives in Carbondale, Illinois, had been bitten twice that June.

Tiguila went home and the next morning, as she was drinking coffee with her usual supplement of bovine collagen for joint, hair and nail health, the test results came in. She had developed a red meat allergy that’s activated by tick bites. “I immediately dumped that coffee down the sink,” says Tiguila. She started avoiding all mammal products — the main way to manage this rising and occasionally life-threatening allergy.

Known as alpha-gal syndrome, the condition arises when the immune system reacts to a certain sugar molecule, called alpha-gal, that’s found in red meat. Symptoms range from a mild rash or stomach upset to anaphylactic shock; in 2025, alpha-gal syndrome [was blamed for the death](https://www.jaci-inpractice.org/article/S2213-2198(25)00953-5/fulltext) of an otherwise healthy 47-year-old man. The syndrome has only recently been characterized and is still not fully understood. Though Tiguila, who is a nurse, was aware of the allergy, she says she still failed to connect her rash to her meaty meals and earlier tick bites.

As [ticks have spread](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/health-disease/2022/lyme-other-tickborne-diseases-rise) northward, so too have alpha-gal diagnoses. Up to 450,000 people in the United States [may have been affected](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7230a2.htm) since 2010, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates.

“It’s emerging as one of the top adult-onset food allergies,” says Onyinye Iweala, an allergist and immunologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

Sandra Tiguila, who acquired alpha-gal syndrome after being bitten by ticks, frequently walks her dogs in this wooded area near her home in Carbondale, Illinois. _Credit: Sandra Tiguila_

**Odd, Even for an Allergy**

Allergies are often mysterious, but this one is extra weird. “Alpha-gal follows none of the rules that I was taught in training about how a food allergy behaves,” says Maya Jerath, an allergist and immunologist at Washington University in St. Louis and one of Tiguila’s physicians. For example, unlike with other food allergies, where reactions are immediate, alpha-gal symptoms often show up hours after eating meat.

And, strangely, the allergy often arises after a tick bite. In the early 2000s, Jerath recalls, Australian allergist and clinician Sheryl van Nunen first shared tales on the scientific-conference circuit of patients with a delayed allergic reaction to red meat after tick bites. “Nobody believed her,” Jerath says.

The eventual unraveling of the mystery would happen on the other side of the world, where immunologist Thomas Platts-Mills, unaware of van Nunen’s findings, was pursuing two parallel projects in his lab at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville. In one, his group was collecting blood samples from people claiming weird meat sensitivities. In the other, they were investigating patients’ strange reactions to the cancer drug cetuximab. It would take both projects to crack the case, recalls Scott Commins, an allergist who was then part of the lab and now works at the University of North Carolina.

First, the cancer strand. Cetuximab is a drug designed to stick to cancer cells and block their overzealous growth. It was first approved to treat colorectal cancer in 2004, but as its testing and use spread, an odd pattern appeared. In the Southeastern United States, more than one in five patients [had allergic reactions](https://ascopubs.org/doi/pdf/10.1200/JCO.2007.11.7812) to the drug — hives, difficulty breathing and even anaphylaxis.

It took about a year and a half, Commins recalls, but Platts-Mills’ group found the culprit. People who reacted badly to cetuximab, they discovered, had blood loaded with proteins called IgE antibodies. When activated inappropriately, IgE causes allergies. The cancer patients with the allergic reactions to cetuximab had IgE antibodies that were [reacting specifically to the sugar alpha-gal](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa074943), the researchers reported in 2008.

Now, humans (and many other primates) [don’t make alpha-gal](https://www.cell.com/cell-host-microbe/fulltext/S1931-3128(20)30680-6). But most mammals do. It’s one of several [sugars that cells attach to proteins](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/living-world/2026/role-of-glycome-biology) to regulate their final structure and function. And cetuximab, like many drugs, is manufactured in lab-grown mouse cells. These cells had attached alpha-gal molecules to the cetuximab. That’s what triggered the allergic reactions in the cancer patients.

But it only happened in some of the people taking the drug. Why them? And why only in the Southeastern United States?

The next clues came from the lab’s other work, on meat sensitivities. This puzzle, of course, also involved exposure to tissues from non-primate mammals — so the researchers hypothesized that this allergy had the same cause as the drug reactions. Sure enough, they found that people with meat sensitivity also had elevated IgE antibodies to alpha-gal, causing a “[novel and severe food allergy](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0091674908019313),” the team reported in 2009.

The allergy is bizarre for several reasons. There’s the delay that van Nunen had noticed. And food allergies are typically triggered by protein: egg protein, nut protein, etc. While some carbohydrates have been linked to mild allergies, a sugar causing such severe reactions was unheard of, says Jeffrey Wilson, an allergist and immunologist at UVA Health in Charlottesville, Virginia.

Plus, [food allergies](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-immunol-042718-041621) were supposed to be all-or-nothing: A person allergic to peanuts will always react to peanuts. Not so with alpha-gal. For example, some people react to meat alone; others might be bothered by dairy or other mammal products, such as gelatin in cosmetics or medications.

Because those products are common, people are exposed to alpha-gal all the time. The sugar can even be made by natural gut bacteria. In other words, most people have no problem with alpha-gal. Platts-Mills, Commins and colleagues were still missing an explanation for why only some people developed this odd sensitivity.

So Commins led a study of people with and without meat allergy to see what the allergic ones had in common. Might they have been exposed to some kind of fungus, or maybe a worm? No, and no.

Then, a key clue emerged from a colleague down the hall. He’d had the meat allergy and joined the study, but had been doing well, so he dared to eat a sausage. Big mistake: He had a bad reaction. Testing showed his alpha-gal IgE had risen to “freakishly high levels,” Commins recalls.

The colleague also had itchy spots — from recent tick bites. That got the team thinking. Commins went back to his meat-sensitive subjects to ask if they’d had tick bites. Most of the nearly 200 people answered yes. The team then learned of [van Nunen’s work](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19413526/), published in 2009, bolstering confidence that they were on the right track. Everything pointed to a tick link: The regions where people had alpha-gal antibodies overlapped with the range of the lone star tick; people who got bitten developed more alpha-gal antibodies, and people with those antibodies often also had antibodies to other lone star tick proteins, the team [reported in 2011](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0091674911003447).

It took several strands of evidence to determine that tick bites can trigger an allergic reaction to the alpha-gal sugar.

Later, biologist Shahid Karim of the University of Southern Mississippi in Hattiesburg and colleagues found alpha-gal [in lone star tick salivary glands](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2019.01056/full). The final clincher implicating ticks came in 2023: Commins and collaborators at the CDC reported that people with alpha-gal syndrome were more than [11 times more likely](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1081120622019639) to recall finding a tick on their body than those who didn’t have the allergy.

Around the world, about a dozen tick species are now associated with alpha-gal allergy. In the United States, the lone star tick is the major player, and it’s [spreading northward](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMp1911661), helped by warmer temperatures and exploding populations of deer that the tick feeds on.

**Mysteries Remain**

Given the expanding health concerns, the CDC has [pledged $10 million](https://simpler.grants.gov/opportunity/ff5a4871-c76a-47b7-8b85-e9ad732f85b3) to support alpha-gal surveillance and awareness among health providers and the public. Scientists, meanwhile, have lingering questions about how the mysterious allergy works.

The pathway from tick bite to meat allergy remains murky. Commins, who [hosts a podcast](https://open.spotify.com/show/033w7oZjV5pp96WpWRib2I) about alpha-gal syndrome, speculates that the body can treat alpha-gal as either something to tolerate or something to react to. The route of exposure seems to be key: Alpha-gal in the gut, from food or bacteria, seems to promote tolerance. But exposure via the skin is a great way to trigger an allergic reaction. That reaction can overshadow the tolerance, often temporarily, Commins says. This hypothesis fits some of the allergy’s features: A strong reaction to the initial bite, or getting lots of bites, boosts risk. Fresh tick bites can also exacerbate or reactivate the sensitivity.

Tick bites can prime the body’s immune system to perceive the alpha-gal sugar as a threat.

Researchers don’t really know why certain ticks cause the allergy and others don’t. One possibility: Perhaps the lone star tick’s taste for human blood, combined with, as Commins notes, its wickedly long skin-piercing mouthparts, underlie this species’ proclivity to incite allergy.

Also puzzling: Some people get tick bites and don’t develop the allergy, and some alpha-gal patients don’t report any history of tick bites. Some people have high levels of IgE antibodies to alpha-gal but can enjoy cheeseburgers freely. Others are sensitive to meats but have low concentrations of the allergic IgE.

Karim, for his part, is trying to figure out what causes some tick victims’ immune reactions to flip from alpha-gal tolerance to allergy. Some research suggests that blood type is a risk factor. Type B blood proteins contain a structure similar to the alpha-gal sugar, and this could promote tolerance, making people with type B or AB blood [less likely to develop IgE antibodies to alpha-gal](https://www.jacionline.org/article/S0091-6749(09)02593-7/fulltext).

Another unresolved question is the odd symptom delay. Wilson speculates that it could be explained if the alpha-gal sugar is hooked to meat fats, rather than meat proteins. Fats take longer for the body to digest and transmit into the bloodstream, so only then would the alpha-gal sugar gain the notice of immune cells.

For some people, their elevated IgE levels will drop and the allergy will go away. In others, it lingers. And sometimes it seems to morph into a generalized disorder where people have allergy-like symptoms even when they avoid meat, says Iweala.

For now, there are no specific therapies for alpha-gal. Allergists can suggest antihistamines and offer EpiPens to thwart a reaction. Some prescribe Xolair (omalizumab), a general allergy treatment that can minimize symptoms if a person encounters alpha-gal. To avoid activating or exacerbating alpha-gal syndrome, the best approach is to avoid tick-ridden areas or use insect repellents like picaridin on skin and permethrin on clothing.

And Commins hopes to create a better treatment. It’s known that an immune signaling molecule called IL-4 is key to the allergic response. He’s in discussions with pharmaceutical companies to test a treatment that would interrupt this IL-4 messaging.

Better therapeutics would certainly be welcome. Alpha-gal syndrome can cause anxiety, since mammal-derived products are ubiquitous and hard to avoid. Tiguila, when she was first diagnosed, went into a label-checking frenzy; she almost threw a bag of prunes across the room because it contained a possibly mammal-derived additive.

A number of factors can influence whether a person will develop an allergy to the alpha-gal sugar.

After visiting the Washington University clinic and being advised to relax around foods that didn’t bother her, Tiguila calmed down. She still enjoys the great outdoors but is careful to slather on insect repellent first.

She recently received more good news: In August of 2026, her blood tested negative for IgE antibodies against alpha-gal, suggesting that her allergy might be gone. Her physicians prescribed a reintroduction protocol they had developed for patients who hit this milestone. She started with an ounce of filet mignon, a low-fat cut, and amped up the exposure from there. “I’ve successfully returned many people to eating meat again,” Jerath says. In one study, her protocol [worked for all 19 participants.](https://www.jaci-inpractice.org/article/S2213-2198(25)01132-8/fulltext)

Add Tiguila to that total: As of late September, she is back to her usual diet. “I’m very grateful to be cleared and not have to be so cautious,” she says.

title: The Fire Inside Me
content:
New Year’s Eve 2019 on the far south coast of Australia was a day without dawn. At nine that morning, the sun was obscured by bushfire smoke rendering the land dizzyingly dark at the height of antipodean summer, like a midday solar eclipse. As one of the region’s obstetricians would painfully discover in the weeks that followed, the black morning skies turned out to be an augur of grievous climate consequences suffered by the unborn.

This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from _Nautilus_.  
To get it in print, **[join by Nov 30](https://nautil.us/hotissue?utm_source=beehiiv&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=issuerelease-issue69-t1-202611&utm_term=free)**.

Photos from that Australian day show a hellish, red-tinted world: hundreds of people in bright summer attire evacuated to strips of beach typically postcard picture-perfect. But the photos fail to capture the heat, a 104 degrees Fahrenheit stew that barely cooled at night. Nor do they show the 62 mile-per-hour gale force winds that fanned flames into explosive thunderclouds, injecting smoke from burning gum trees 100,000 feet up into the stratosphere. There, the sun-warmed smoke generated a self-sustaining vortex five miles tall and 600 miles across with its own ozone hole, the likes of which atmospheric scientists had never before seen.

December 2019 had been abnormally dry and hot across Eastern Australia, especially in New South Wales, where temperatures ran almost 6 degrees F hotter than the monthly average. By New Year’s Eve, 100 fires raged across the region, most sparked by dry lightning. The flames grew explosively, triggering 38 firestorms over eastern Australia that grew with the ferocity of volcanic eruptions. Atmospheric scientists later dubbed the spate of fire-induced pyrocumulonimbus thunderstorms that erupted the “Australian New Year Super Outbreak.”

On the ground, conditions tightened, like a violin string ready to snap. There were more fires, bigger fires, faster fires. “They were coming from the north and coming up from the south, and there was this impending sense of threat,” said Michael Holland, the senior obstetrician in Moruya, a beach town four hours south of Sydney, with a population of about 4,300. With highways out of town cut off and no safe egress, thousands had to shelter in place. “Every park had camper vans, mobile homes, caravans,” Holland recalled. “There were people with goats and there were people with sheep. It was almost biblical: people evacuating, waiting for the ark to be built.”

Holland was in his 60s and a fixture of Moruya’s maternity ward, located in the town’s small general hospital. A ruddy-faced, quiet-spoken man who embodies the stoic character of his country, Holland quickly teamed up with an ER physician to set up triage at his hospital.

Moruya had lost power, and the hospital emergency generator barely had power to run an X-ray machine. Food and meds were spoiling in lukewarm fridges and stalled sewage pumps stagnated toilet bowls. Holland’s own home was under evacuation, so he and his family slept on the floor of his medical practice for five days. It felt like the apogee of a longer arc of misery as the Black Summer burned its way through the season. Smoke lingered in an ever-present ceiling all summer long. “For months we didn’t see the stars,” Holland said.

By mid-January, rain and cooler temperatures finally provided respite. In the following weeks, as smoke finally cleared from the skies, Holland discovered something that surprised and then shocked him. Three women in their third trimesters experienced “fetal death in utero,” or stillbirths.

In a typical year of practice, Holland saw about 350 births at the Moruya hospital, of which one might be a stillbirth, typically from prematurity or fetal abnormalities. In the recent cluster of three stillbirths, each of the placentas was highly abnormal. The tissue was thin, calcified, grainy to the touch. Typically, placentas resemble a pizza-shaped liver, all spongy and deep burgundy.

Although Holland didn’t know it at the time of the fires, in late 2019 a team of Belgian scientists had published a study that claimed, for the first time, to find evidence of black carbon particulates on the fetal side of the placenta. Later studies found particulates from air pollution in fetal cord blood, too, proof that the microscopic constituents of wildfire smoke can pollute not just a mother’s blood but her fetus’ too.

Public health experts now estimate that some 15,000 pregnant Australians and their fetuses were exposed to the Black Summer fires. While most were spared the brutal losses suffered by Holland’s patients, the smoke’s impact was measurable. Pregnant people are especially vulnerable to poor air quality since they breathe for two, taking in about 50 percent more air in their day to meet growing oxygen demands. One analysis of pregnant women found those exposed to the Black Summer fires in early- to mid-pregnancy were more likely to have their water break before 37 weeks, a leading cause of preterm birth. That same study found that the 2019 Black Summer bushfires were associated with an 11 percent higher risk of stillbirth, although the incidence was mercifully small enough as to preclude statistical significance.

Today, Holland is retired from his medical practice and is a member of the Australian parliament. He spoke to me about his work as an obstetrician with a natural buoyancy, describing how shortly after clamping the umbilical cord, the uterus, previously ballooned to cocoon the baby, deflates and loosens the placenta, which birth practitioners typically examine. This practice of midwives and obstetricians gathering round the placenta always conjured ancient history for him. “It reminds me of some fortune teller in ancient Rome looking at the entrails or something,” he said.

It’s no longer the melting poles or ocean-logged Pacific Islands that are on the front lines of climate change, but our very own human bodies. And nowhere is that bodily toll so unfair, and unacknowledged, as when it is exacted in utero.

**BLACK SUMMER:** Fallout from summer bushfires in New South Wales, Australia, in 2019, shocked a local obstetrician. _Credit: Aussie Bush / Shutterstock_

In earlier days of the climate change discourse, circa the early 2000s, the warming in store was presented as a straight-up temperature increase, like the thermostat of a house slowly rising. In Vancouver, my hometown, we were forewarned about shrinking ice caps and melting glaciers from the rising mercury, but never the concomitant burning.

For most of my adult life, the air around me cleared as fuel standards and regulations cleaned up exhaust—a welcome improvement given that air pollution is a major environmental cause of death worldwide. But over the past decade of escalating wildfire seasons, that positive trend is now being reversed as worsening wildfire smoke dials back those gains.

Since 2016, fire smoke has erased about 25 percent of the multi-decade progress made across North America to reduce air pollution. Across the western United States during bad fire seasons, fire smoke accounts for half of the fine particulate matter in the air that people breathe over a year.

Just as concerning, there is increasing evidence that the fine particulate matter from wildfires is a more toxic and carcinogenic beast than other sources of it, like automobile traffic. A 2021 study of emergency and urgent care pediatric admissions in San Diego County in California found it to be ten times more harmful to children’s respiratory health than air pollution from other sources. One hypothesis is that as the smoke travels vast distances over many days, its molecular make-up transforms to become more chemically unstable and reactive, increasing its toxicity to human cells.

There is a misconception that when a baby is developing in utero, they are protected in the womb, floating free of the worries that await outside the cocoon of their pregnant parent’s body. But evidence suggests they are far from inured and are the most vulnerable among us. Miniscule airborne pollutants in the smoke, whether they are near the source or lofted into the atmosphere where they can travel the world, can enter the parent’s bloodstream through the lungs. Those fine particulates can cross the placental barrier and circulate in the fetus.

In 2018, Amy Padula, a professor in the department of obstetrics, gynecology and reproductive science at the University of California, San Francisco, was completing her first grant application to study wildfire smoke and preterm birth when smoke from the Camp Fire, California’s deadliest blaze to date, descended on San Francisco. She was pregnant with her second child at the time. Her daughter, a toddler, was soon talking like Darth Vader from the airborne irritants, Padula said.

Padula remembers just how incapable she felt when it came to protecting her family from the smoke—their rental was drafty and the smoke didn’t just set up shop across the bay, but indoors too. The HEPA filters they ran to scrub the air proved inadequate in their leaky apartment. It really hit home. Here she was, pregnant, trying her hardest to protect her growing family from the malignant air, and articulating in her grant application the very questions that applied to the exact situation she found herself in. How is this affecting my unborn child? How is this affecting our children’s lungs as they’re developing?

Over the next five years, Padula and her colleagues found consistent links between wildfire smoke exposure and preterm birth, including one analysis of more than 5 million births in the state of California. “We’ve also looked at it in terms of, ‘Is it the duration of exposure or the cumulative number of days you’re exposed?’” said Padula, now interim director of the Program on Reproductive Health and the Environment at UCSF. “Basically, just more is worse.” She and her colleagues have published research on associations between wildfire smoke and structural birth defects in California as well as with increased risk of severe maternal morbidity. “These exposures are increasing and we’re not necessarily well equipped to protect this vulnerable group,” she said.

Up the coast in Vancouver, the British Columbia Centre for Disease Control has been conducting its own extensive research into the effects of wildfires on the unborn. So far, its studies have documented evidence of lower birth weight, higher rates of respiratory infections in baby’s early years, and first trimester pregnancy termination linked to wildfire exposure in the province.

“It’s clear these exposures during pregnancy and early life have long-lasting health impacts, probably lifelong health impacts,” Sarah Henderson, the center’s scientific director of environmental health, told me in 2023. “As a society, we’re not nearly focused enough on what these climatic changes mean for people who are young or who are not even born right now.”

**FOREBODING STUDY:** Smoke obscures Pyramid Lake in Alberta, Canada, in 2017. More than 30,000 children were studied by public health officials in Western Canada that year. _Credit: Arthur Greenberg / Shutterstock_

In July 2015, I was pregnant with my daughter. My husband and I had left town for a short vacation to one of the islands that face Vancouver across the Salish Sea where we had recently finished building our off-the-grid cabin. The week-by-week fetus app on my phone told me that our baby was the size of a green olive. The air was soupy and muggy. A giant, uncontrollable fire burned in the Elaho Valley, famed for its old growth trees, across the water and over the coastal slopes facing us.

We had slept with the cabin windows open, lulled to sleep by the lapping of waves, but awoke to air that was pungent and wrong, as if someone had just doused a campfire with water, spluttering ash into our faces. Every surface of the cabin was coated in fine white ash. It was astonishing, and loathsome. I had never felt such a potent, intuitive desire to not breathe. I wanted to claw at my throat, where the taste of damp, smoldering newspaper was lodged. Instead, I began to wipe everything down.

More than 30,000 children who were in utero during British Columbia’s record wildfire season of 2017 were later studied by public health scientists. Those whose mothers lived in areas with the worst smoke exposure were likelier to be born smaller and preterm; they were also sicker, developing croup, laryngitis, and bronchitis at higher rates than other children. The researchers also detected a small increase in first-trimester pregnancy loss. The toll on those born as those fires raged also runs steep; a study by Health Canada and other federal Canadian departments estimated that in parts of the province hardest hit by the 2017 fires, wildfire smoke from that one fire season alone reduced life expectancy by a full year.

Vancouver emerged better than other parts of the province that summer, but I still remember days on end of cloying, singed air and an orange hue to the light at all hours. Our house didn’t have air conditioning, and like many Vancouver homes, we would simply open our windows at night to cool down and ease our slumber. But when the air outside was clogged with smoke, visibility obscured beyond several hundred meters, we faced the choice of either sweltering at night in oppressive heat, or opening our windows and breathing in the singed, yet cool, night air as we dreamt.

By early 2019, when my belly grew with her younger brother, my husband drilled giant holes through our home to Macgyver HEPA-filtered intake fans. We were lucky the summer he was born, and his tiny lungs were spared, but it was a temporary reprieve. By the time he was three, there had been multiple times when his outdoor daycare was cancelled because of wildfire smoke. Just as unfortunate, there were times the kids simply breathed in bad air all day. By the time he and his sister were in elementary school, the fire season was lasting longer into September and starting earlier in the summer. There were days that the school kids sheltered in their gym over recess and lunch because the air outside was too poisonous to play in.

In the fall of 2025, I learned that Michael Kobor, Canada Research Chair in Social Epigenetics at the University of British Columbia, was conducting a province-wide survey to study blood from newborns exposed to the last decade of fire seasons while in utero. He wanted to apply his lab’s expertise in studying DNA methylation—a natural biological process in which a chemical group (methyl) is added to the underlying genetic code—to understand if wildfire exposure was being embedded in the developing fetus, and to what end. Previous work in the field of epigenetics has demonstrated that environmental exposures can become biologically embedded through DNA methylation, which can be associated with disease risk later in life.

In a preliminary study focused on a couple hundred blood samples, Kobor’s lab found that exposure to wildfire activity was associated with changes to DNA methylation in a newborn’s blood. His team is now doing further analyses to see if these changes are associated with later health outcomes such as respiratory illness, mood and anxiety disorders, and ADHD. Kobor has also launched a new and ambitious project, the BC Wildfire Study. The goal is to recruit 1,200 children who were in utero between 2016 and 2024 and further study how wildfires are associated with changes in DNA methylation and health and developmental outcomes.

“I think really what we’re trying to answer is: Is there a biological legacy that’s carried into the next generation from prenatal wildfire exposure?” Kobor told me from his laboratory at the BC Children’s Hospital Research Institute. “How can we collectively see what’s happening at that molecular level and harness that information to ensure that as these wildfires happen and increase in severity and frequency, our next generation continues to go strong.” The scientists hope to publish the first findings related to the study in 2028.

**EVACUATION:**A father and daughter head to an evacuation center in Australia in 2019. _Credit: Joachim Zens / Shutterstock_

The year after Rachel Carson’s “Silent Spring” was published in _The New Yorker_, and shortly afterward as a world-changing book, Carson gave the opening lecture to the Kaiser Foundation Hospitals and Permanente Medical Group’s annual symposium in San Francisco in 1963. It was the last public address she ever gave, as she passed away the following year from breast cancer.

Much of Carson’s lecture is timeless in its wisdom and as far as final words go, they resonate decades later. Our failings as she diagnosed them in 1963 remain just as true today. A recurrent theme was her reflection on our stubborn reluctance to concede that humans are as much at risk from the harms posed by environmental pollutants as fish in a river or a flock of birds in a marsh. “It seems to me to imply a sort of rejection of our past—a reluctance or an unreadiness to accept the fact that man, like all other living creatures, is part of the vast ecosystems of the earth, subject to the forces of the environment,” she told her audience.

For decades, we have been turning the dials on those “forces of the environment,” running a planet-scale experiment that has ripened the conditions for extreme weather. How could we expect to experiment with the flammability of Earth’s ecosystems without anticipating that we would become subjects of the test ourselves? We have given Mother Earth her fever. Did we think we would be spared her symptoms?

In November 2025, I went onto the website of the BC Wildfire Study and filled out the screening survey to submit my son as an official participant in the blood analysis of children who were in utero between 2016 and 2024. Days later, I received an email informing me that he had been accepted. Lab researchers, I was told, would retrieve his newborn blood sample from the bowels of BC Children’s Hospital, punch out a tiny hole in the card with his dried blood spots, extract DNA from it, and process it through a few additional steps to measure the level of DNA methylation in it.

I filled out an online survey. Had we ever seen a doctor about asthma? We had. Had he ever been treated for pneumonia and upper respiratory infections? He had. Weeks later, a buccal swab to collect additional DNA arrived in the mail to compare how methylated his DNA was now at age six compared to levels at birth.

I felt unsettled as I looked at the swab kit. I reflected on how the first years of my kids’ lives had been among the hottest on record, each strewn with record-breaking this and unprecedented that. I wondered about how these climate-related crises had and would affect them as they grew up. As I reviewed the steps with my son, I explained why our participation in the study was important (it’s to help scientists understand how smoke affects kids so they can better protect them).

I wanted him to get the gist of it, but not more than that. This was a burden I very much wanted to spare him, yet here I was actively seeking out the encumbrance of that knowledge myself. Then again, it hardly felt like a choice; I had to understand the thing that was threatening my child.

In the run up to Christmas 2025, the Pacific Northwest was clobbered by successive freight trains of atmospheric rivers dumping days of rain in a matter of hours. The rain was warm and it came down in heavy, fat drops, like a tropical monsoon. The weather systems crossing the Pacific Ocean toward us were subtropical in nature, meteorologists noted. The latest system that emptied its firehose over us drowned the Skagit Valley in Northwestern Washington State. Watersheds in Southern British Columbia were soon inundated, and Vancouver was cut off from the rest of Canada as the Trans-Canada highway was flooded and the highway route north was closed due to the high risk of mudslides. I barely batted an eye. I braved the rain to find a mailbox to send in my son’s DNA. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Is the Privatization of Space Sustainable?
content:
Gone are the days when hurling payloads into space was a purely governmental effort. There is an ever-growing constellation of private startups engaged in a final frontier make over.

The privatization of space is truly on the move. News of the latest SpaceX launch of its Starship and successful return-to-launch pad recovery as well as other private space sector achievements are becoming near-daily events.

**Read more: “**[**The Deep Ocean Is a Global Public Good**](https://nautil.us/the-deep-ocean-is-a-global-public-good-1238459)”

Low Earth orbit is already crowded with commercial satellites, and the vision of what’s to come includes commercial space stations, networks of floating data centers, constellations of power-beaming satellites, made-in-space pharmaceutical factories, gas-and-go refueling facilities, even rubbernecking space tourists in search of the most exotic of destinations.

But as we blast off into this uncertain future, what laws, international agreements, or treaties might guardrail the development? Are we rushing headlong into conflict? Or are we floating peacefully into a shared and harmonious collaboration in the heavens?

Some futuristic forecasters see space as an evolving economic zone that may one day span the distance between Earth and the moon.

Amazon founder and space capitalist, Jeff Bezos, is projecting that millions of people will dwell in the vacuum of space in just two decades time. Indeed, that shift could occur much faster than many foresee, buoyed by governmental investments in exploring and exploiting the cosmos and powered by a potent mix of advances in artificial intelligence and robotics. Will this result in a Wild West of private space ventures?

Matt Weinzierl, professor of business administration at the Harvard Business School and co-author of _Space to Grow: Unlocking the Final Economic Frontier_, says that “privatization” is not really the right term for what’s happening. “The government is not getting out of space. In fact, the government is still an absolutely central player,” he says. “I call it ‘commercialization,’ because the big change is the rise of market forces in space.”

Indeed, the infusion of private capital has already changed the complexion of humanity’s incursions into space. In October, the Office of Space Commerce—an arm of the United States Department of Commerce—and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) released a [report](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.1500-39.pdf) titled, “Building an In-Space Circular Economy.”

That report centers on the fact that, “traditional space activities have followed a linear, single mission model in which spacecraft are designed, launched, operated, and ultimately disposed of through atmospheric reentry or relocation to graveyard orbits.” Thanks to the growth of the commercial space sector, this “take-make-use-dispose” paradigm is increasingly challenged by the economic and operational realities of long-duration space activity.

A “circular space economy” is an alternate approach, underscores the report, that could reduce dependence on terrestrial resupply by extending the lifetimes of assets in space through the inspection, servicing, repair, reuse, repurposing, and recycling of space systems.

Casting an eye to the future, the report says that building an in-space circular economy will require coordination among policy, finance, technology, and standards organizations. That’s prelude to a functioning circular space economy that depends on a persistent physical and digital infrastructure. “Servicing hubs, modular platforms, transportation networks, manufacturing and recycling facilities, power generation, and communications must operate as parts of an interconnected system,” states the report.

**UNDER NEW OWNERSHIP:** Commercial space group, Vast, is set to launch the world's first commercial space station in 2027. _Credit: Vast_

A long-time witness to the evolution of low Earth orbit from a barren frontier into an emerging marketplace is Jeffrey Manber, a special representative to the chairman and CEO at Voyager Technologies, a defense technology and space solutions company. “Even at this early stage in commercial development, low Earth orbit services are fulfilling critical national security needs and, at the same time, acting as a foundation for emerging markets,” he says.

Manber says he’s confident that in 10 years, low Earth orbit will be far more populated with services and platforms than today. Commercial space markets, he adds, take decades to develop and reach emerging status, and only after governments make the initial commitment to invest in such frontiers. In his view, there will be a number of orbiting space stations in different inclinations, owned by different organizations and companies focused on different markets, with some focused on in-space research and manufacturing. Others will be hotels, warehouses, and fuel depots, some U.S.-owned while others are supported by other nations.

And, critically, Manber suggests, that growth will spill over to cis-lunar—the space between the Earth and the moon—and onto the surface of the moon itself.

It will still take time before there is advancement from a government lunar program propelled by companies and private capital to one where the government is truly one customer of many, adds Manber.

“For me it is clear. The next commercial frontier is cis-lunar and the lunar surface marketplace,” Manber notes, “one that is international in nature, with competing transportation, habitats, communications, minerals extraction, power and oxygen and agricultural generation goods and services.”

Indeed, multiple nations are targeting the moon as a snug and cozy extraterrestrial camper spot for ever-longer stays of human visitors. The potential uses of the moon include mining Helium-3, a scarce resource on our world but imbedded in the lunar topside and ideal for quantum computing fueling fusion reactors on Earth.

NASA itself has [speculated](https://www3.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/artemis_economic_competitiveness_impacts_5-18-2022_tagged.pdf) that from the 2030s and beyond entirely new markets will emerge. “Once companies have established a toehold on the lunar surface and in cislunar orbit, they may provide services such as transportation to destinations in the Earth-Moon system, electrical power, rocket fuel depots, water extraction, and resource mining.

This projected commercialization of space, in Earth orbit and outward to the moon is undergirded by almost 60 years of space law.

Michelle Hanlon is executive director of the Center for Air and Space Law at the University of Mississippi School of Law. She is also a permanent observer of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space. “We are commercializing the infrastructure through which space is reached, used, and increasingly relied upon. Article II of the UN’s Outer Space Treaty of 1967 prohibits national appropriation of outer space, including the moon and other celestial bodies,” she says. “It does not expressly prohibit private property, nor does it tell us exactly which private rights may arise as commercial activity develops.”

The legal framework leaves room for commerce, Hanlon argues, but it does not clearly define where legitimate private rights end and impermissible national appropriation begins. And that is where the history of other shared domains—think Antarctica or the open ocean—becomes useful, she suggests, although such analogies must be considered carefully.

**PEACEFUL COLLABORATION:** British Antarctic Survey’s Halley Research Station in Antarctica, the unpopulated continent where about 30 countries adhere to the Antarctic Treaty of 1959 to conduct peaceful scientific research. _Credit: Sam Burrell, British Antarctic Survey_

About 30 countries engage in activities—mostly of the scientific variety—in Antarctica. All 30 are parties to the 1959 Antarctic Treaty System. Perhaps that bleak, foreboding polar panorama can serve as a template for working on the moon—for how diverse nations can play nice in a shared sandbox.

“Antarctica demonstrates that states can cooperate without resolving every underlying disagreement. Its system uses advance notice, information sharing, inspections, scientific cooperation, and environmental review,” Hanlon says. “But resource mining is prohibited there, so the dynamic is very different.”

Earth’s oceans host several different models and mechanisms of cooperation functioning simultaneously, adds Hanlon. “The high seas retain broad freedoms,” she says. “The deep seabed is governed through the common heritage principle, and newer agreements add environmental and procedural obligations without placing every ocean activity under one centralized authority.”

But none of those systems can simply be transplanted into space, explains Hanlon. “Antarctica is a singular continent with a distinctive history of territorial claims and a prohibition on resource extraction,” she says. “The ocean has physical, ecological, and commercial characteristics that differ sharply from orbit or the moon.”

Space, then, will require its own, unique legal framework. “The lesson is not that space should copy one of them,” Hanlon continues. “The lesson is that governance can and should be tailored to the particular resource, activity, and risk.”

The Outer Space Treaty gives us tools, including freedom of exploration and use, non-appropriation, due regard, and reciprocal access to stations, installations, equipment, and vehicles on celestial bodies. “But those tools still leave significant room for interpretation, and first movers will shape how they are applied in practice,” Hanlon points out.

**COSMIC COOPERATION:** International dignitaries signed the United Nations Outer Space Treaty at a White House ceremony on January 27, 1967. _Credit: United Nations_

So are existing laws robust enough to adequately govern the expansion of space commerce?

Space law works in layers, Hanlon says. The Outer Space Treaty provides the basic principles and tools to help implement them. Countries are free to explore and use space. They cannot claim it as national territory, and they must give due regard to the interests of other countries, as detailed in the Treaty.

Still, governments face a practical question: Who oversees what a particular company actually does once it achieves orbit or lands on the moon? “Closing that gap, through clear authorization and ongoing supervision, lets commercial activity expand without leaving responsibility behind,” Hanlon suggests.

And how is the UN’s 60-year-old Outer Space Treaty holding up as we enter this new era of commercializing space? Are countries adhering to it?

The Treaty itself remains remarkably successful, says Hanlon, when you see it for what it is: a set of tools rather than a rigid set of rules. “It has never been amended, and it almost certainly never will be. Negotiators working at the height of the Cold War went as far as they could,” she says. “They gave us freedom of use, non-appropriation, and the concept of due regard.” But those drafters could not have imagined, she adds, a space domain that is so crowded and bristling with commercial potential. So there are real gaps.

“The work of the UN's Action Team on Lunar Activity Coordination and its Space Resources Working Group are all attempts to take the tools the Treaty gave us, especially due regard and the promotion of international cooperation and transparency, and operationalize them for the activities now underway,” Hanlon notes. “The foundation is solid. The work now is to keep building on it.”

There is the vacuum-packed truism that nobody can hear you scream in space.

Nevertheless, the economic bottom line for the heavens above is how space business will be regulated and just how loud the commercial “Ka-Ching” will sound in the years and decades ahead. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: New Species of Flying Frog Discovered in Indonesia
content:
New species can be discovered in [all sorts of ways](https://nautil.us/a-new-species-emerges-from-a-9-5-million-year-old-whale-carcass-1286464). In the case of _Rhacophorus kurniatia_, a type of Asian flying frog that’s only just been identified, it involved a trek deep into the Mekongga Mountains in Indonesia, to a secluded lake where thousands of frogs had congregated.

“We were moving up the mountain, and we came across this big pond covered in these green frogs,” Alan Hitch, one of the authors of [a new study](https://doi.org/10.11646/zootaxa.5900.4.3) about _Rhacophorus kurniatia_, explained in a [statement](https://www.ucdavis.edu/news/new-asian-flying-frog-species-identified-indonesia). “They were all over. You don’t really see frogs in big congregations like that. This was something super special.”

The lake where the frog species was discovered. _Credit: UC Davis MWFB Archives, NIH-ICBG Expeditions_

They were quickly identified as being flying frogs, from the _Rhacophorus_ genus. The large webbed feet, for gliding between trees, were the main giveaway. Further analysis revealed something not seen in other _Rhacophorus_ species, though: The frogs deposit their eggs in gelatinous masses hanging above or near water, rather than in the typical foamy nests.

Offspring are born in a gelatinous matrix. _Credit: Wahyu Trilaksono/Museum Zoologicum Bogoriense_

Distinctive, pointed snouts, as well as differences in the calls made by the frogs, confirmed that this was a species that hadn’t been observed and documented before.

“The team looked at hundreds and hundreds of specimens of frogs to describe the new species,” study author Andrew Engilis Jr. said in a [statement](https://www.ucdavis.edu/news/new-asian-flying-frog-species-identified-indonesia). “Sometimes species can look the same, but their behavior is different and their genetics are different—these are called cryptic species. This frog is an example of that. It looks very similar to other _Rhacophorus_, but its genetics and behavior show that it’s very distinctive.”

The identification of _R. kurniatia_ is the culmination of four years of work on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, which is close to Borneo. Expeditions carried out by the researchers led them from sea level to the highest mountain peaks—with the new flying frog species discovered some 6,100 feet above sea level.

The late researcher Hellen Kurniati, at work in the field. _Credit: UC Davis MWFB Archives, NIH-ICBG Expeditions_

And there’s a bittersweet reason for the naming: The flying frog’s scientific name was chosen as a mark of respect for renowned herpetologist Hellen Kurniati, who died in 2024. She was one of the leading researchers studying amphibians and reptiles in Indonesia. She also helped to discover the new species that now shares her name. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: You Likely Have Genes That Affect How Well Your Medications Work— Testing for Them Could Improve Treatment
content:
All people carry differences in their DNA that could [affect how they respond to medication](https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.adt8040), according to my team’s newly published research. Moreover, 1 in 4 already take a medication their body processes differently because of their genetics.

Clinicians often take a trial and error approach to prescriptions. Two people take the same medicine at the same dose. One starts feeling better, but the other experiences side effects or sees little benefit. For some medications, part of the reason behind that difference in response is written in a person’s DNA.

The [field of pharmacogenomics](https://www.cdc.gov/genomics-and-health/pharmacogenomics/) studies how variations in your DNA contribute to how your body processes and responds to medicines. For instance, genes can influence how quickly your [liver breaks down a drug](https://theconversation.com/why-prescription-drugs-can-work-differently-for-different-people-168645) and how long it stays in your bloodstream.

But using [genetic testing to guide prescriptions](https://theconversation.com/can-at-home-dna-tests-predict-how-youll-respond-to-your-medications-pharmacists-explain-the-risks-and-benefits-of-pharmacogenetic-testing-209312) is not yet routine. Part of the problem is a lack of large population data to study this approach more broadly. Clinicians don’t know when it’s best to order genetic testing. And because most genetic research has been [done on people of European ancestry](https://theconversation.com/uncovering-the-genetic-basis-of-mental-illness-requires-data-and-tools-that-arent-just-based-on-white-people-this-international-team-is-collecting-dna-samples-around-the-globe-185997), researchers know less about how common key gene variants are in everyone else.

**Genetic Variants and Drugs**

To improve the diversity of pharmacogenomic data, my team of researchers [and I](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=LKG31OkAAAAJ&hl=en) analyzed the whole genome sequences and health records of nearly 100,000 participants in the [All of Us Research Program](https://www.nih.gov/allofus). All of Us is an effort from the National Institutes of Health to study the health of 1 million or more people across the U.S. and its territories, with a focus on groups historically left out of biomedical research.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ti50nS7B5vI)

We examined 16 genes with well-established links to how someone responds to different medications, pairing this data with electronic health records to identify which drugs participants had already taken.

We found that every participant [carried at least one relevant genetic variant](https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.adt8040), and many carried several. Around 99.5% of participants had a genetic variant for which the Food and Drug Administration or medical guidelines recommend a different drug or change in dose for certain medications.

Even more telling, about 24% had taken a drug that is [affected by a genetic variant](https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.adt8040) they carried. Common examples included drugs used to reduce excess stomach acid, such as omeprazole and pantoprazole, and statins used to lower cholesterol levels. Because health records can be incomplete, our results likely underestimate the actual prevalence of these gene-drug interactions.

These findings can help improve the databases clinicians and researchers use routinely in research. We identified [17,704 previously unreported variants](https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.adt8040) in the regions of these genes that encode proteins. Computer models predicted that about a quarter may have significant effects on how the body processes drugs.

Our team also reported the frequencies of hundreds of genetic variants linked to drug response for people from genetic ancestries that previously had incomplete data.

**Improving Precision Medicine**

Overall, our research shows that DNA variation is very common, and broader genetic testing may help optimize the medications clinicians prescribe to patients. It’s also an example of how big initiatives such as the All of Us Research Program can advance [precision medicine](https://theconversation.com/personalized-cancer-treatments-based-on-testing-drugs-quickly-leads-to-faster-treatment-better-outcomes-221469).

However, this study doesn’t prove testing would improve outcomes for each of these people. Additionally, genes are only one factor; age, kidney and liver function, and other medications also [affect how the body processes drugs](https://theconversation.com/why-prescription-drugs-can-work-differently-for-different-people-168645).

Still, I believe the direction of the research is clear. Pharmacogenomics can provide potentially relevant benefits for many people who take medications. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

The [ACX Prediction Contest](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/acxmetaculus-prediction-contest-2026) is back for 2027, the fifth year Metaculus has hosted. There’s a $10,000 prize pool for the best forecasters, plus $3,000 for question suggesters. The ten people who contribute the most to the roughly 35 questions Metaculus selects will split the $3,000, with prizes from $150 to $700. Past question sets are in the [2025](https://www.metaculus.com/tournament/ACX2025/) and [2026](https://www.metaculus.com/tournament/ACX2026/) contests.

This year is also an opportunity to see how far AI forecasting has come, as the best are now competitive with strong human forecasters. AI forecasting agents are welcome to enter and eligible for prizes, and Metaculus will post its own AI forecasts on every question.

A good question suggestion has an objective answer that we’ll know by the end of 2027, with a source that settles it. “Will 2027 be especially hot?” is less good than “Will NASA’s GISTEMP data rank 2027 as the warmest year on record?”

[Suggest questions here](http://forms.gle/L8NXoQpAkXkdvDRF6) by November 30. The contest will open in early 2027.

There were good reasons to think it's the hardest of the Millennium problems, even before this year. The other problems, with the possible exception of the Riemann Hypothesis, were either conjectures that seemed like they might be true for intuitive or heuristic or empirical reasons, or they're strongly tied to geometric or physical intuition, or actually both in most cases.

The only reason it's such a famous problem is because the answer is very consequential and it's resisted solution for 50 years. (Those are good reasons for it to be a famous problem, of course.) I'm far from an expert on computational complexity (though I did take Stephen Cook's complexity course back in the day), but I've generally assumed the likeliest answer is that in fact P != NP but that it's undecidable.

I am not the original poster, but personally I would consider a solution to P vs NP to be orders of magnitude more surprising than a solution to the Riemann Hypothesis. The RH has seen steady progress over time, with substantial advances even in the last 5-10 years.

For P vs. NP, the progress in proving unconditional lower bounds in the last 60 years is zero. Even for sorting, the best known lower bound is Omega(n),(*) so our best argument is "you need at least to read the input". And it's not just sorting, the set of problems where we can prove ANYTHING better than "Omega(length of input plus output)" is basically empty. Not for sorting, not for 3SUM, not for factoring, heck, not even for SAT.

(*) There is a famous lower bound of Omega(n log n), but this only holds for comparison-based algorithms. This is typical: we are able to say a few things for severely restricted classes of algorithms, but even there it usually does not go beyond the "obvious" information-theoretic bounds.

So, I think we need to be careful to distinguish two separate things.

Thing one: how does one solve the SPECIFIC sorting problem I care about right now? If I care about integers then I can use whatever operations integers support, writing as much nested if spaghetti code as needed. It may well be possible to do this in linear time.

Thing Two: how do I write a “generic” sorting algorithm? That is, how can I sort ANYTHING that can be sorted at all? Since a generic algorithm doesn’t know anything about what I’m sorting, it has no choice but to use comparisons.

If you’re lucky enough, maybe you never need to use a generic sorting algorithm because you can always find a clever way to take advantage of how your data is special.

But that’s just you being clever and lucky. A generic algorithm still has its hands tied.

Why do you say it's unlikely it's undecidable? It's long been my top candidate for "actually-important math question that's undecidable".

Relatedly, it's fun to consider exactly which variety of undecidable it is. Of course, it could be "undecidable, and its decidability is undecidable". This is the *only* way the Riemann Hypothesis could have turned out to be undecidable (I'll need to think of a new example now)--if we had been able to *show* RH was undecidable, that would mean a search for roots would never turn up a counterexample, which means there could be no counterexamples, which would tell us it was true.

But it's conceivable we could prove P vs NP is undecidable. If we know it's undecidable, we know we will never find a proof that P=NP, and in particular we would never find an algorithm for an NP-complete problem that we could prove was polynomial in time. But we might find algorithms that *actually are* polynomial time, we could just never be sure they were polynomial (or we could never be sure they always gave correct answers). Or maybe it's undecidable, and we can show it's undecidable, and in fact P != NP. In that case, we would just never know if there exist polynomial time algorithms for SAT. We might wrongly suspect one of our correct algorithms was actually polynomial time, or we might wrongly suspect one of our polynomial time algorithms was actually correct, but we'd never know.

Not the GP post, but I can try to explain why I think it's very unlikely P v NP is undecidable. (In rationalist tradition of quantifying beliefs, I'd put it at 1%.)

First, to be clear, "undecidable" needs to be anchored to a certain set of axioms. ZFC is usually the working standard in math, but there are systems considerably stronger than ZFC that are generally believed to be arithmetically sound (i.e. prove only true statements about the integers--and importantly, P v NP can be phrased purely in terms of integers). IIUC, Lean uses a system slightly stronger than ZFC.

The reason why I think P v NP is unlikely to be undecidable in ZFC is basically because ZFC is absurdly strong for proving arithmetic statements. Peano Arithmetic resolves basically every natural statement in number theory, i.e., stuff that doesn't originate from proof theory. Even though mathematicians sometimes go beyond ZFC (e.g. Grothendieck universes) in their proofs, such as for Fermat's Last Theorem, number theory theorems have always been reducible to Peano Arithmetic.

Far stronger than Peano Arithmetic is second-order arithmetic. Far stronger than second-order arithmetic are weak set theories, and far stronger than weak set theories is ZFC.

It just gets really hard for me to see what about P v NP would require such high order reasoning that Peano Arithmetic wouldn't cut it, much less set theory. Even though P v NP has some connections with foundations of mathematics, it doesn't really feel at all similar to the examples of known-independent problems. Known-independent problems originate either directly from self-referential problems (i.e. encoding axioms into number theory), or rapidly growing functions that use so many iterations of diagonalization that it doesn't fit into Peano Arithmetic's induction capabilities. [Edit:] P v NP is really just a question about a truth tables of size 2^2^N, and this object doesn't feel so complicated to me that it shouldn't be approachable with Peano Arithmetic's tools.

(I realize this may not be convincing, because it relies a lot on my personal mental models I got while studying proof theory. But hopefully it gives some insight why one might think independence is unlikely.)
